entries.title: ACCOUNT
entries.body:
In HD (hierarchical deterministic) wallets, an account represents a derivation layer at depth 3 according to BIP-0032. Each account is numbered sequentially starting from `/0'/` (hardened derivation, so actually `/2^31/` or `/2 147 483 648/`). It is at this derivation depth that the famous `xpub` are found. Nowadays, a single account is generally used within an HD wallet. But initially, they were designed to segregate various categories of use within the same wallet. For example, if we take a standard derivation path for an external Taproot (P2TR) receiving address: `m/86'/0'/0'/0/0`, the account index is the second `/0'/`.

![BIP-84 tree with an arrow pointing to the Accounts level at depth 3, where the wallet's xpubs are defined.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/compte/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY
entries.body:
Refers to the ability of a protocol rule update to maintain compatibility with earlier versions. This means the changes are designed so that old nodes (nodes running versions prior to the rule change) can still interact with the network and follow the chain with the most accumulated work. Old nodes must therefore reject neither the new blocks nor the new transactions.

Backward compatibility greatly reduces the probability that an update fragments the network, thus avoiding the division of nodes into subgroups on different chains. To ensure compatibility with earlier versions of the protocol, an update must make the existing rules stricter or introduce new ones. This principle is what defines a “soft fork”. Conversely, if an update loosens existing rules or removes some of them, it will not be backward compatible. It will then be a “hard fork”.

entries.title: C++
entries.body:
A general-purpose programming language, evolved from C, known for its power and flexibility. Used for complex software development, it supports object-oriented programming and offers rich features for managing memory and system resources. 

Bitcoin Core, the majority implementation of the Bitcoin protocol, is written in C++. This is a legacy of Satoshi's very first client, which was also written in this programming language. To guarantee strictly consistent node behavior across the network, notably to avoid *forks*, it was decided not to change languages since 2009.

entries.title: CAHOOTS
CAKE WALLET
entries.body: An open source wallet available on iOS, Android, macOS, Linux and Windows, initially designed for Monero and later extended to Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies. CakeWallet stands out in the Bitcoin ecosystem for its integration of privacy features, notably support for *Silent Payments* and *Payjoin v2*. The wallet is non-custodial and allows the user to keep control of their private keys. It offers a built-in exchange service to convert between different cryptocurrencies, as well as native Tor integration to strengthen privacy at the network level.

entries.title: CANAAN
entries.body: A company founded in 2013 by Nangeng Zhang, specializing in the manufacture of bitcoin mining machines. Canaan is the originator of the AvalonMiner, the very first ASIC designed specifically for Bitcoin mining. Based in Singapore, Canaan became in 2019 the first company in the mining ASIC sector to be listed on the NASDAQ.

entries.title: CANDIDATE BLOCK
entries.body: A candidate block is a block being created by a miner taking part in the mining process of the Bitcoin system. The candidate block is a temporary data structure that contains transactions waiting to be confirmed, but does not yet have a valid proof of work (*Proof-of-Work*) to be added to the blockchain. The miner selects the transactions to include in the candidate block based on various factors, such as the associated transaction fees and block size constraints. Once the transactions are selected, the miner generates the block header, which includes the version, a digest of the transactions (Merkle root), a timestamp, the hash of the previous block, the difficulty target and a nonce. The miner then tries to find a hash of its header that satisfies the current target difficulty. To do so, it modifies the nonce present in the header. It can also modify other information present in its candidate block. This is the proof-of-work mechanism. If the miner succeeds in finding a valid hash, the candidate block becomes a valid block and is broadcast to the network to be added to the blockchain.

entries.title: CASA
entries.body:
An American company offering multisig bitcoin security solutions for individuals. Casa offers a service where private keys are split between the user (on their *hardware wallet* and their phone) and Casa (which holds an emergency recovery key). This 2-of-3 or 3-of-5 model makes it possible to secure one's funds without a single point of failure, while still having a recovery option in case a device is lost.

Casa also offers a built-in inheritance protocol. It is used through a mobile application and the service operates on a subscription basis with different security tiers.

entries.title: CASASCIUS
entries.body:
Physical coins that contain bitcoins, created starting in 2011 by Mike Caldwell. Each Casascius coin embeds a private key concealed under a tamper-proof hologram, which allows its holder to access the associated bitcoins.

The coins were available in several denominations (1 BTC, 10 BTC, 25 BTC, 100 BTC...) and feature a design with a golden “B”. They made it possible to physically transfer bitcoins without going through the network, simply by handing the coin to the recipient.

In November 2013, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) considered this activity to be a form of money transmission that requires registration. Mike Caldwell then stopped selling preloaded coins, while continuing to produce blank coins. Casascius coins have become sought-after collector's items.

entries.title: CASHU
entries.body: An open-source Chaumian electronic money protocol, similar to David Chaum's eCash system, but which works on Bitcoin and the Lightning Network. More precisely, Cashu is inspired by a variant of eCash proposed in 1996 by David Wagner called “*Chaumian ecash without RSA*”. Cashu can be used on custodial wallets so that the server can identify neither the owners of the funds nor the details of the transactions, thus offering an improvement in privacy. Users can generate Cashu tokens in exchange for bitcoins, which are signed by the server without knowing the user. The tokens can then be transferred between users instantly, privately and without fees.

entries.title: CBDC
entries.body:
Acronym for “*Central Bank Digital Currency*”. It is a digital form of fiat money issued and controlled directly by a central bank, unlike conventional bank deposits, which are created by commercial banks.

CBDC projects are being developed in many countries: the digital euro in Europe, the digital yuan (e-CNY) in China, or the *Sand Dollar* in the Bahamas. They can operate on centralized ledgers or use technologies inspired by blockchains, but remain under the total control of the issuing authority.

Supporters see them as a tool for modernizing payments and for financial inclusion. Critics, notably in the Bitcoin community, raise major privacy risks: a CBDC would potentially allow the state to monitor, block or place conditions on every transaction of citizens, constituting an unprecedented tool of financial control. CBDCs are fundamentally different from Bitcoin, which is decentralized and censorship-resistant.

entries.title: CBTC - CITREA BITCOIN
entries.body: The native representation of bitcoin on the Citrea rollup. cBTC (*Citrea Bitcoin*) is the native currency used to pay *gas* fees and carry out transactions on the Citrea network. It is obtained by depositing BTC on the main Bitcoin chain via the Clementine bridge, which locks the funds and issues an equivalent amount of cBTC on the rollup. It can be converted back into BTC at any time via Clementine's *peg-out* mechanism.

entries.title: CENSORSHIP RESISTANCE
entries.body:
A property of a system that makes it capable of operating without any entity being able to prevent legitimate participants from using it. In the context of Bitcoin, censorship resistance means that no government, company or individual can block a valid transaction or prohibit a user from accessing the network.

This property rests on several fundamental characteristics of Bitcoin: the decentralization of the network (thousands of nodes spread around the world), the absence of a central authority able to filter transactions, and the proof-of-work operation, which makes the inclusion of transactions depend solely on the fees offered by the sender.

Censorship resistance is considered one of Bitcoin's most important value propositions, particularly in authoritarian regimes where citizens may have their bank accounts frozen or their transactions blocked. It fundamentally distinguishes Bitcoin from centralized payment systems and CBDC projects, where an authority can decide at any time to exclude users.

entries.title: CET
entries.body: Acronym for “*Contract Execution Transaction*”. It is a transaction specific to a DLC that allows the final settlement between the parties based on the outcome of a future event. When the oracle publishes a signature corresponding to the outcome of the event, the parties use this signature to complete and unlock the CET that sends the funds to the winning party. The signed CET is then broadcast on the network, and the winner receives the bitcoins owed to them according to the terms of the smart contract. All the other potential CETs, which would have been executed in the case of different outcomes, become obsolete and are abandoned.

entries.title: CGMINER
entries.body: *Open-source* mining software initially developed for CPU and GPU. CGminer allows users to manage and optimize their mining operations, with features such as *multi-threading*, management of multiple pools and real-time performance monitoring. The software is no longer really maintained these days, but it has been replaced by Braiins' *open-source* BOSminer project, which was rewritten from scratch in Rust.

entries.title: CHACHA20-POLY1305
entries.body:
An authenticated encryption algorithm with associated data that combines the ChaCha20 stream cipher and the Poly1305 message authentication code. It takes as input a 256-bit key and a 96-bit nonce, and produces a ciphertext accompanied by a 128-bit authentication tag that guarantees both the integrity and the authenticity of the data.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, ChaCha20-Poly1305 is used in the P2P v2 transport protocol (BIP-0324) to encrypt communications between nodes of the network. It is also used in the transport layer of the Lightning Network (BOLT-08), where the Noise framework uses it to encrypt and authenticate the messages exchanged between peers after the initial *handshake*.

entries.title: CHAIN CODE
entries.body:
In the context of hierarchical deterministic (HD) derivation of Bitcoin wallets, the chain code is a 256-bit cryptographic salt value used to generate child keys from a parent key, according to the BIP-0032 standard. The chain code is used in combination with the parent key and the index of the child to deterministically generate a new key pair (private key and public key) without revealing the parent key or the other derived child keys. 

There is therefore a unique chain code for each key pair. The chain code is obtained either by hashing the wallet seed, and taking the right half of the bits. In this case, we speak of a master chain code, associated with the master private key. Or, it can be obtained by hashing a parent key with its parent chain code and an index, then keeping the right bits. We then speak of a child chain code. 

It is impossible to derive keys without knowing the chain code associated with each parent pair. It makes it possible to introduce pseudo-random data into the derivation process to ensure that the generation of cryptographic keys remains unpredictable for attackers while being deterministic for the holder of the wallet.

entries.title: CHAINALYSIS
entries.body: An American company founded in 2014, specializing in blockchain analysis and the tracing of cryptocurrency transactions. Chainalysis provides software and services to governments, law enforcement, financial institutions and exchange platforms to detect and track the flow of funds on public blockchains, notably Bitcoin's. Its tools make it possible to track funds and to identify links between transactions and real-world entities. To do so, Chainalysis exploits chain analysis heuristics.

entries.title: CHAINCODE LABS
entries.body: A Bitcoin research and development center founded in 2014 by Alex Morcos and Suhas Daftuar in New York. Chaincode Labs funds and employs Bitcoin Core developers, and organizes training programs for open source contributors to the Bitcoin protocol.

entries.title: CHAINSPLIT
entries.body: A name sometimes given to a natural fork, that is, a temporary split of the blockchain resulting from the near-simultaneous broadcast of several blocks by different miners at the same height.

entries.title: CHAINSTATE/
entries.body: The technical name given to the folder used to store the UTXO set on Bitcoin Core. It is therefore actually a synonym for “UTXO set”.

entries.title: CHAINWAY LABS
entries.body: The company behind the development of Citrea, the first ZK rollup deployed on Bitcoin. Founded with the goal of building infrastructure solutions for Bitcoin, Chainway Labs specializes in zero-knowledge proof technologies applied to the Bitcoin ecosystem. The team notably develops Citrea and its bidirectional bridge Clementine, based on BitVM. All the code produced by Chainway Labs is open source, published under the GitHub account `chainwayxyz`.

entries.title: CHAINWORK
entries.body:
A metric that quantifies the total number of hashes expected to produce a given blockchain. Chainwork serves as the criterion for determining the valid chain: nodes always follow the chain that has the greatest chainwork, and not simply the one that contains the most blocks. The calculation relies on the difficulty target of each block. For a given block, the average number of hashes needed to obtain a hash less than or equal to the target is:
```math
\frac{2^{256}}{cible\ +\ 1}
```
The total chainwork of a chain is the sum of these values for each block, from the genesis block up to the block in question. Since difficulty varies over time, two chains of identical lengths can have a very different chainwork: a chain mined under high difficulty will have a higher chainwork than a longer chain built under artificially low difficulty.

In the first version of the software, Satoshi Nakamoto used the number of blocks as the criterion for selecting the valid chain. This approach was vulnerable to manipulation, because an attacker could build a longer chain by keeping the difficulty at a low level. Chainwork replaced this metric to ensure that the valid chain is indeed the one that required the most actual work. The value is accessible via the command `bitcoin-cli getblock` in the field `chainwork`.

entries.title: CHAMPION - BIP
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin Core development (the majority implementation of Bitcoin), the champion is the person who writes and takes charge of managing a BIP (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal). The champion is responsible for writing the BIP following the formal process, defending it before the community, answering questions and guiding discussions to refine the proposal. They also work to obtain the consensus necessary for the BIP to be accepted and implemented. They can

*The champion is also sometimes called the “author”. Their name can in fact be found noted after the “Author” header in BIPs. There can sometimes be several champions for the same BIP.*

entries.title: CHANGE
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin transactions, refers to the UTXO created with the remaining funds after the actual payment has been satisfied. When UTXOs with a quantity of bitcoins greater than the amount needed for the actual payment and the transaction fees are used as inputs, the surplus is a UTXO sent back to an internal wallet address, called a change address. Change represents this UTXO. For example, if you want to pay for a baguette that costs `4 000 sats` with a UTXO of `10 000 sats`, you will create in your transaction a change output of `6 000 sats` (if transaction fees are neglected).

![Transaction with an input UTXO of 10,000 sats, an output of 4,000 sats for the payment and a change output of 6,000 sats.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/change/assets/image-1.png)

*Even though it is very rarely used, one could also speak of “monnaie” (rendu de monnaie) to refer to change.*

entries.title: CHANGE AVOIDANCE
entries.body:
A UTXO management strategy that consists of selecting a transaction's inputs in such a way as to eliminate or minimize the need to create a change output. The goal is to match the sum of the inputs as closely as possible to the payment amount plus the transaction fees.

The main benefit of this approach is privacy. A change output is often identifiable by chain analysis tools and provides information for tracing funds over time. By eliminating it, the information available to an outside observer is reduced, you avoid revealing information in the future via the CIOH, and you can also mislead chain analysis.

Some wallets implement this strategy automatically in their coin selection algorithm.

entries.title: CHANNEL ACCEPTOR
entries.body: An LND mechanism that allows defining custom logic to automatically accept or reject incoming channel opening requests. When a remote peer proposes to open a channel, the request is passed to the *channel acceptor*, which replies with `TRUE` or `FALSE`, optionally accompanied by an error message intended for the initiator.

entries.title: CHANNEL ANNOUNCEMENT
entries.body:
A message broadcast on the Lightning network to signal the existence of a new payment channel to the other nodes. This message is what distinguishes a public channel from a private one: only channels whose partners choose to broadcast a *channel announcement* appear in the network graph and can be used by third parties to route payments.

The message contains, among other things, the identifiers of the two partner nodes, the reference to the on-chain funding transaction, and the signatures of both parties. Upon receiving this message, the other nodes of the network verify that the partners do hold the funds in the funding transaction before adding the channel to their local database. The *channel announcement* is part of the Lightning Network's *gossip* protocol, which ensures the propagation of information about the network topology between peers. Channels that do not broadcast this message are called “private” (or “unannounced”) and remain invisible in the graph.

entries.title: CHANNEL BREACH
entries.body:
An attempt at cheating on the Lightning Network, in which a peer publishes an old commitment transaction (*commitment transaction*) to try to recover a balance that no longer belongs to them. When such a revoked state is broadcast on the blockchain, the counterparty has a period defined by the *timelock* to detect this fraud and publish a justice transaction that allows them to recover all of the channel's funds.

The detection of a channel breach can be handled directly by the node if it is online, or delegated to a *watchtower* that monitors the blockchain continuously. If the breach is not contested before the *timelock* expires, the cheater keeps the funds unduly recovered.

entries.title: CHANNEL FACTORIES
entries.body: An advanced mechanism currently being worked on for Lightning, allowing the creation and management of multiple payment channels from a single UTXO. Channel factories use `n-of-n` multisig addresses so that a group of users can collectively hold a single UTXO. From there, they can open and close payment channels between themselves without additional on-chain transactions, except when they wish to withdraw their funds from the factory. This method would make it possible to considerably reduce the costs and the space taken up on Bitcoin for Lightning transactions. In practice, this means that operations that would normally require on-chain transactions for each channel opening or closing can be performed off-chain, with security guaranteed by the ability to publish the unpublished transactions if necessary. To borrow the words of David A. Harding, channel factories can be described as Lightning channels used to generate other Lightning channels.

entries.title: CHANNEL JAMMING
entries.body:
A denial-of-service attack on the Lightning Network that consists of blocking the routing capacity of one or more payment channels for a prolonged period, preventing honest nodes from routing payments. The attacker sends a fictitious payment to themselves through a series of intermediate channels, then refuses to finalize or cancel the HTLC, which immobilizes the routing nodes' funds at no cost to the attacker.

The attack comes in two variants:
* *Liquidity jamming* (described as early as 2015 under the name “loop attack”) exploits the leverage effect of multi-hop routing: with `x` bitcoins, an attacker can lock up to `20x` bitcoins on a path of 20 channels.
* *Slot jamming* exploits the limit of 483 simultaneous HTLCs per channel: by sending 483 micro-payments, an attacker saturates the available slots with minimal capital.

Several mitigation approaches are being explored: fees paid in advance (*upfront fees*) by the sender, a local reputation system between peers, proof-of-funds certificates (*stake certificates*), and reputation tokens. bLIP-0004 proposes an HTLC approval mechanism (*HTLC endorsement*) as a first concrete measure. No definitive solution has yet reached consensus.

entries.title: CHANNEL LEASE
entries.body: A contract to open a Lightning channel for a fixed duration, negotiated via the Lightning Pool platform. A liquidity buyer (*taker*) pays a premium to a seller (*maker*) so that the latter opens a channel of a defined capacity and duration, expressed in number of blocks. The seller commits to keeping the channel open for the entire duration of the lease.

entries.title: CHANNEL POINT
entries.body: The unique identifier of a Lightning channel on the Bitcoin blockchain. It consists of the TXID of the channel's funding transaction followed by the index of the corresponding output, in the form `txid:output_index`. For example: `a3f2...b7c:0` designates the first output of the funding transaction. The *channel point* makes it possible to find the on-chain transaction that established the channel and serves as a reference in node administration commands, for example to close a specific channel or view its details.

entries.title: CHANNEL RESERVE
entries.body:
The minimum amount that each party of a Lightning channel must keep on their side and cannot spend. This reserve guarantees that each participant always has something to lose in the event of an attempted fraud, which makes penalty transactions economically dissuasive.

When a channel is opened, each node imposes a *channel reserve* on its peer, generally set at 1% of the channel capacity (with a floor of 546 satoshis, corresponding to the *dust limit*). For example, in a channel of 1,000,000 sats, each party must maintain at least 10,000 sats on their side. This threshold is defined in the `channel_reserve_satoshis` field during channel negotiation (BOLT-02).

The *channel reserve* slightly reduces the effectively usable capacity of a channel. In the v1 protocol, it can be asymmetric, with each side able to impose a different amount. In the case of *dual funding* (v2), the reserve is set at 1% of the channel's total balance for both parties and is no longer negotiable.

entries.title: CHANNEL.DB
entries.body:
The database used by LND to store the complete state of all of a node's Lightning channels. This file is located in the `.lnd/data/graph/mainnet` directory and contains the list of open channels, the peers' identifiers, the latest commitment transactions for each channel, and the information needed to punish a peer who would attempt to broadcast an old state.

The `channel.db` file changes constantly: every payment, every routing operation, every channel opening or closing modifies its contents. This is why it is not a reliable backup medium in the traditional sense. Restoring an outdated version of `channel.db` exposes the operator to the Lightning protocol's penalty mechanism: peers may consider that an old state is being broadcast and recover all of the channel's funds. The only safe use of `channel.db` for a restoration is direct recovery from a machine that has just crashed, which ensures that the state is indeed the most recent one. For a reliable backup, LND instead offers the SCB (*Static Channel Backup*) mechanism.

entries.title: CHANTOOLS
entries.body:
A command-line tool developed by Lightning Labs that makes it possible to recover funds stuck in Lightning channels when the LND node no longer works properly. Chantools steps in during emergency situations where the standard recovery mechanisms (restoration via *Static Channel Backup*) fail or are not sufficient.

The tool offers about thirty commands covering different recovery scenarios: extraction of a `channel.backup` file from a corrupted database (`chanbackup`), forced publication of a channel's last known state (`forceclose`), sweeping of funds after the timelock expires (`sweeptimelock`), recovery of funds resulting from force closures by the remote peer (`sweepremoteclosed`), or cooperative recovery of zombie channels (`zombierecovery`). Some commands are also compatible with Core Lightning. Using chantools requires the node's seed, but it never leaves the local machine.

entries.title: CHAUMIAN COINJOIN
entries.body:
A coinjoin protocol that uses David Chaum's blind signatures and Tor for communications between the participants and the coordinator's server. The goal of a Chaumian coinjoin is to guarantee to participants that the coordinator can neither steal the bitcoins nor link the inputs and the outputs. 

To do this, users submit their input and a cryptographically blinded receiving address to the coordinator. This address, once unblinded, will be intended to receive the bitcoins as a coinjoin output. The coordinator signs these tokens and sends them back to the users. The users then reconnect anonymously to the coordinator's server with a new Tor identity and then reveal their output addresses in clear text for the construction of the transaction. The coordinator can verify that all these receiving addresses do come from legitimate users, since it previously signed their blinded version with its private key. However, it cannot associate a specific output address with a given input user. There is therefore no link between the inputs and the outputs, even from the coordinator's point of view. Once the transaction is built by the coordinator, it sends it back to the participants, who sign it in order to unlock their input, after having verified that their output is indeed in this transaction. The participants send the signature to the coordinator. Once all the signatures have been collected, the coordinator can broadcast the coinjoin transaction on the Bitcoin network.

![Sequence of a Chaumian coinjoin: sending the input and a blinded output, blind signature, anonymous unblinding via Tor.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/chaumian-coinjoin/assets/image-1.png)

This method guarantees that the coordinator can neither compromise the participants' anonymity nor steal the bitcoins throughout the coinjoin process.

It is difficult to determine with certainty who first introduced the idea of coinjoin on Bitcoin, and who came up with the idea of using David Chaum's blind signatures in this context. It is often thought that Gregory Maxwell was the first to mention it in [a message on BitcoinTalk in 2013](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=279249.0):

> *“Using chaum blind signatures: The users connect and provide inputs (and change addresses) and a cryptographically-blinded version of the address they want their private coins to go to; the server signs the tokens and returns them. The users anonymously reconnect, unblind their output addresses, and return them to the server. The server can see that all the outputs were signed by it and so all the outputs had to come from valid participants. Later people reconnect and sign.”*

Maxwell, G. (2013, August 22). *CoinJoin: Bitcoin privacy for the real world*. BitcoinTalk Forum. https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=279249.0

However, there are other earlier mentions, both of Chaum's signatures in the context of mixing, and of coinjoins. [In June 2011, Duncan Townsend presents on BitcoinTalk](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=12751.0) a mixer that uses Chaum's signatures in a way quite similar to modern Chaumian coinjoins. In the same thread, one can find [a message from hashcoin in response to Duncan Townsend](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=12751.msg315793#msg315793) to improve his mixer. This message presents what most closely resembles coinjoins. A mention of a similar system can also be found in [a message from Alex Mizrahi in 2012](https://gist.github.com/killerstorm/6f843e1d3ffc38191aebca67d483bd88#file-laundry), when he was advising the creators of Tenebrix. The term “coinjoin” itself would not have been invented by Greg Maxwell, but would come from an idea of Peter Todd.

entries.title: CHECKPOINTS
entries.body:
Hashes of specific blocks that were hard-coded in Bitcoin Core. Each checkpoint associated a block height with an expected hash, and any fork below an already synchronized checkpoint was rejected.

Introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto on July 17, 2010 (version 0.3.2), this mechanism aimed to prevent any rewriting of the historical chain, even by an attacker with a majority of the computing power. In practice, checkpoints mainly served as an anti-DoS protection during the IBD: without them, an attacker could exploit the *time warp* bug to overwhelm a new node's memory with millions of minimum-difficulty headers. But these checkpoints did not add any real security to consensus: if checkpoints had to influence the choice of the chain, the system would already be compromised. The last one was added at block 295,000, in April 2014.

Checkpoints were removed in Bitcoin Core 30.0 (October 2025), replaced by the *headers presync* mechanism (August 2022), which verifies a chain's proof of work before storing its headers, eliminating any data hard-coded by the developers.

entries.title: CIOH
frenchAliases: HEURISTIQUE DE PROPRIÉTÉ COMMUNE DES ENTRÉES
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*". It is a heuristic used in the field of chain analysis on Bitcoin that assumes that all the inputs of a transaction belong to the same entity or the same user. When one observes the public data of a Bitcoin transaction and spots several inputs in it, then, if there are no *patterns* or other information that would contradict this, one can estimate that all the inputs of this transaction belonged to one and the same person (or entity).

This analysis heuristic was discovered by Satoshi Nakamoto himself, who mentions it in section 10 of the White Paper:

> "*Some linking is still unavoidable with multi-input transactions, which necessarily reveal that their inputs were owned by the same owner. The risk is that if the owner of a key is revealed, linking could reveal other transactions that belonged to the same owner.*" - Nakamoto, S. (2008). "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System". Retrieved from https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

Even today, CIOH remains the main heuristic used by chain analysis companies, along with address reuse.

![CIOH heuristic: four inputs coming from different transactions are assumed to belong to the same user.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/cioh/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: CIRCULAR REBALANCE
entries.body: A payment that a Lightning node sends to itself along a path going through other nodes of the network. The goal is to move liquidity from one channel to another without opening or closing a channel. For example, if a node has a lot of outbound liquidity on a channel A but lacks outbound liquidity on a channel B, it can send itself a circular payment that goes out through A and comes back through B, thus rebalancing the two channels. This operation has a cost corresponding to the routing fees charged by the intermediate nodes.

entries.title: CISA
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Cross-Input Signature Aggregation*". It is a technical proposal that aims to optimize the size of Bitcoin transactions by reducing the number of signatures required to validate them.

Currently, on Bitcoin, each input of a transaction must have an individual signature in order to be spent. This proves that the owner of the UTXO in question authorizes the transaction. With CISA, the goal is to combine the signatures of all the inputs of a single transaction into one signature that covers all the inputs. This would reduce the size of transactions that have many inputs, and therefore also reduce their fees. It would be particularly useful for people who perform coinjoins or consolidations, while also making it possible to confirm more transactions on Bitcoin without changing the size or interval of blocks. CISA relies on the Schnorr protocol, which allows linear aggregation of signatures. This means that a single signature can prove possession of several independent keys.

However, implementing CISA on Bitcoin is very complex, because it requires deep modifications to the way scripts work. Currently, script verification on Bitcoin is done input by input. Moving to a model where an entire transaction is verified at once, as CISA proposes, is far from a trivial change.

entries.title: CITREA
entries.body: The first zero-knowledge proof rollup (ZK rollup) deployed on Bitcoin, developed by Chainway Labs. Citrea uses a Type 2 zkEVM, built with RISC Zero, which offers full compatibility with the Ethereum virtual machine and allows Solidity developers to deploy their contracts directly on Bitcoin. The system processes transactions off-chain in batches, generates STARK proofs (then wrapped into SNARK proofs) and publishes these proofs directly on Bitcoin, which serves as both the data availability layer and the settlement layer. Citrea's two-way bridge, named Clementine, relies on BitVM2 and operates with a 1-of-N trust assumption: as long as at least one verifier of the bridge is honest, the funds are safe. The native bitcoin on Citrea is called cBTC. The platform also offers ctUSD, a dollar-pegged stablecoin backed by US Treasury bills, issued in partnership with MoonPay and M0. Citrea requires no modification to Bitcoin's consensus rules. The *mainnet* has been live since January 2026.

entries.title: CLARK - COVENANTLESS ARK
entries.body:
A version of the Ark protocol that can be implemented without requiring covenants to be added to Bitcoin via a soft fork. The name "clArk" is the contraction of "*covenantless Ark*". When Ark was initially proposed in May 2023 by Burak Keceli, the protocol required covenants, which were not yet available on Bitcoin. The clArk version, developed starting in 2024, works around this limitation.

In the absence of covenants, clArk emulates the spending conditions by asking all the participants of a round to sign n-of-n multisig transactions. Each participant must sign the entire VTXO tree making up the round, whereas covenants would allow signing only the clauses concerning their own funds. This approach results in a significant overhead in bandwidth, storage and interactivity: all participants must be online simultaneously during the round.

The possible addition of covenants to Bitcoin would substantially improve the protocol: users would no longer need to be connected permanently, the liquidity management of ASPs would be optimized, and the protocol could better handle certain scenarios. ClArk therefore represents a compromise that makes it possible to deploy Ark on Bitcoin as it exists today, without needing to do a soft fork.

entries.title: CLEARNET
entries.body:
Term designating the conventional internet, as opposed to overlay networks such as Tor or I2P. On the *clearnet*, communications travel with identifiable IP addresses, which makes them observable by internet service providers, network operators or any intermediary.

In the context of Bitcoin and the Lightning Network, using the *clearnet* means that a node's IP address is directly visible to its peers and to network observers. Many node operators prefer to connect exclusively via Tor to protect their identity, even though the *clearnet* offers faster and more stable connections. Some hybrid configurations allow nodes to be reachable on both Tor and the *clearnet*.

entries.title: CLEMENTINE
entries.body: Trust-minimized two-way bridge developed by Chainway Labs for the Citrea rollup. Clementine makes it possible to transfer BTC between the main Bitcoin chain and Citrea (BTC ↔ cBTC) without relying on a conventional trusted multisig. The protocol is based on BitVM2 and operates with a 1-of-N trust assumption: it is enough for a single participant in the group of verifiers to be honest for the funds to be protected against theft. For a deposit (*peg-in*), the user sends BTC to a Taproot address encoding two spending paths: one path allows the signers to move the funds to a vault (*vault*), the other allows an automatic refund after a *timelock* if the bridge does not respond. For a withdrawal (*peg-out*), the user burns their cBTC on Citrea, then an operator advances the funds in BTC on Bitcoin and is subsequently reimbursed from the vault, provided that no challenger proves fraudulent behavior through a challenge mechanism using BitVM2. Clementine is open source.

entries.title: CLI
entries.body: Acronym for “*Command Line Interface*”, or “interface en ligne de commande” in French. It is a method of interacting with software that relies on entering text commands in a terminal or console. The CLI differs from the GUI (graphical user interface), which offers pointing methods of interaction (with the mouse) and interactive visual elements.

entries.title: CLIENT-SIDE VALIDATION
entries.body: Process by which each party (client) verifies a set of privately exchanged data, according to the rules of a protocol. In the case of the RGB protocol, this exchanged data is grouped together in what are called consignments. Unlike the Bitcoin protocol, which requires all transactions to be published on-chain, RGB makes it possible to store publicly only commitments (anchored in Bitcoin), while the bulk of the contract information (transitions, attestations, proofs) remains off-chain, shared only between the users concerned.

entries.title: CLN - C-LIGHTNING
entries.body: Former name of the Core-Lightning implementation.

entries.title: CLN - CORE-LIGHTNING
entries.body: Major implementation of the Lightning Network protocol written in the C and Rust languages. Developed by Blockstream, Core-Lightning is designed to be lightweight and high-performing. It stands out for its modular architecture, which allows developers to easily add custom features. This implementation was renamed in 2022. Its original name was previously “C-Lightning”.

entries.title: CLONE
entries.body: In the context of Git, consists of creating a local copy of a remote repository. This operation downloads the entire repository, including all branches and the commit history. As a Bitcoin user, you may have to use this command when downloading software.

entries.title: CLUSTER
entries.body: In the context of chain analysis, a cluster is a set of receiving addresses that are associated with the same entity by an analyst. Using various heuristics, it is possible to detect *on-chain* activities that appear to originate from a single person or organization. This grouping of activities forms what is called a *cluster*. The goal of chain analysis is often to identify an entry point into this cluster, thereby making it possible to link all of these activities to some form of real-world identity.

entries.title: CLUSTER MEMPOOL
entries.body:
Proposal to overhaul mempool management in Bitcoin Core. The cluster mempool organizes unconfirmed transactions into “clusters” (*clusters*): sets of transactions linked by parent-child relationships. Within each cluster, a linearization algorithm pre-computes the optimal mining order and groups the transactions into “chunks” (*chunks*) sorted by decreasing fee rate.

This overhaul fixes an inconsistency in how the mempool currently works. Transaction selection for mining uses the highest ancestor fee rate, whereas eviction uses the lowest descendant fee rate. Since these two heuristics are not symmetrical, it can happen that the best transaction in the mempool is evicted first. With the cluster mempool, block building and eviction become exactly inverse operations: chunks are included from most profitable to least profitable, and evicted in the reverse order.

This approach is viable thanks to the limit on cluster size, which replaces the former ancestor and descendant limits. Since optimal chunks never cross the boundaries between clusters, adding a transaction only requires recomputing its own cluster. The fee rate of each chunk then serves as a unified score for all mempool operations: block building, eviction, RBF evaluation, transaction relay and fee estimation.

entries.title: CODEX32
entries.body:
Scheme for encoding and backing up BIP-0032 seeds on paper, specified in BIP-0093. Codex32 stands out from existing alternatives through the ability to manually verify the integrity of a backup, without using any electronic device.

The system relies on Shamir's secret sharing: the seed can be split into several shares (*shares*), of which only a configurable subset (quorum) is needed to reconstruct the secret. Each share is encoded as a Bech32 character string that includes a checksum (*checksum*). It is this checksum that makes Codex32 unique: it can be computed and verified entirely by hand using lookup tables or rotating paper templates called “volvelles”. The operation remains laborious, but it guarantees that a user can audit their backups in a completely offline environment and without any digital component.

Codex32 supports 128-bit and 256-bit seeds. It is an alternative to SatoshiLabs' SLIP39 scheme, which also offers Shamir sharing but requires an electronic device for verification. Core Lightning integrated support for Codex32 for seed backup and restoration in 2023.

entries.title: COIN CONTROL
entries.body:
Feature found in some Bitcoin wallet software, which gives users the ability to manually select the specific UTXOs to use as inputs to make a transaction. In other words, coin control offers the possibility of choosing precisely which pieces of bitcoins will be spent. This feature is similar to the action of choosing a specific coin from your wallet to pay for your baguette. 

Coin control is particularly useful for managing your transaction fees and for improving your privacy. Indeed, by specifically selecting the UTXOs to consume, users can avoid merging UTXOs from different sources, which could reveal information about all of their funds (CIOH). This feature often goes hand in hand with the ability to label transaction outputs.

entries.title: COINBASE
entries.body:
The coinbase transaction is a special and unique transaction included in every block of the Bitcoin blockchain. It is the first transaction of a block and is created by the miner who successfully found a header that validates the Proof-of-Work (*Proof-of-Work*), that is, one that is less than or equal to the target.

The coinbase transaction mainly serves two purposes: allocating the block reward to the miner and adding new units of bitcoin to the circulating money supply. The block reward, which is the economic incentive for miners to contribute to carrying out the proof of work, comprises the fees accumulated for the transactions included in the block and a determined amount of newly created ex-nihilo bitcoins (block subsidy). This amount, initially set at 50 bitcoins per block in 2009, is halved every 210,000 blocks (approximately every 4 years) during an event called the “halving”.

The coinbase transaction differs from regular transactions in several ways. First, it has no input, which means that no existing transaction output (UTXO) is consumed in it. Second, the signature script (`scriptSig`) for the coinbase transaction generally contains an arbitrary field allowing additional data to be incorporated, such as custom messages or mining software version information. Finally, the bitcoins generated by the coinbase transaction are subject to a maturity period of 100 blocks (101 confirmations) before they can be spent, in order to prevent the potential spending of non-existent bitcoins in the event of a chain reorganization.

*There is no French translation of “Coinbase”. It is therefore accepted to use this term directly.*

entries.title: COINJOIN
entries.body:
Coinjoin is a technique for breaking the traceability of bitcoins. It relies on a collaborative transaction with a specific structure of the same name: the coinjoin transaction. Coinjoin transactions improve the privacy of Bitcoin users by making transaction analysis more difficult for outside observers. This structure makes it possible to mix several coins into a single transaction, making it difficult to determine the links between input and output addresses.

The general operation of coinjoin is as follows: several users who want to mix each deposit an amount as an input of a transaction. These inputs will come out as several outputs of the same amount. At the exit of the transaction, it is therefore impossible to determine which output belongs to which user. Technically, there is no link between the inputs and the outputs of the coinjoin transaction. The link between each user and each UTXO is broken, in the same way as the history of each coin.

![Coinjoin with five participants: the UTXOs of Alice through Emma form five outputs of 100,000 sats indistinguishable from one another.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/coinjoin/assets/image-1.png)

To allow coinjoin without any user losing control of their funds at any time, the transaction is first built by a coordinator and then passed on to each user. Each of them then signs the transaction on their own side, checking that it suits them, and then all the signatures are added to the transaction. If a user or the coordinator tries to steal the funds of the others by modifying the outputs of the coinjoin transaction, then the signatures will be invalid and the transaction will be rejected by the nodes. When the registration of the participants' outputs is done using Chaum blind signatures to avoid the link with the input, it is called a “*Chaumian coinjoin*”.

This mechanism increases transaction privacy without requiring any changes to the Bitcoin protocol. Specific coinjoin implementations, such as Whirlpool, JoinMarket or Wabisabi, offer solutions to facilitate the coordination process between participants and strengthen the efficiency of the coinjoin transaction. Here is a coinjoin transaction as an example: 

```text
323df21f0b0756f98336437aa3d2fb87e02b59f1946b714a7b09df04d429dec2
```

It is difficult to determine with certainty who first introduced the idea of coinjoin on Bitcoin, and who had the idea of using David Chaum's blind signatures in this context. It is often thought that Gregory Maxwell was the first to mention it in [a message on BitcoinTalk in 2013](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=279249.0):

> *“Using chaum blind signatures: The users connect and provide inputs (and change addresses) and a cryptographically-blinded version of the address they want their private coins to go to; the server signs the tokens and returns them. The users anonymously reconnect, unblind their output addresses, and return them to the server. The server can see that all the outputs were signed by it and so all the outputs had to come from valid participants. Later people reconnect and sign.”*

Maxwell, G. (2013, August 22). *CoinJoin: Bitcoin privacy for the real world*. BitcoinTalk Forum. https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=279249.0

However, there are other earlier mentions, both of Chaum signatures in the context of mixing, and of coinjoins. [In June 2011, Duncan Townsend presents on BitcoinTalk](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=12751.0) a mixer that uses Chaum signatures in a way quite similar to modern Chaumian coinjoins. In the same thread, one can find [a message from hashcoin in response to Duncan Townsend](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=12751.msg315793#msg315793) to improve his mixer. This message presents precisely what most resembles coinjoins. A mention of a similar system can also be found in [a message from Alex Mizrahi in 2012](https://gist.github.com/killerstorm/6f843e1d3ffc38191aebca67d483bd88#file-laundry), when they were advising the creators of Tenebrix. The term “coinjoin” itself was reportedly not invented by Greg Maxwell, but would come from an idea of Peter Todd.

*The term “coinjoin” has no French translation. Some bitcoiners also use the terms “mix”, “mixing” or even “mixage” to refer to the coinjoin transaction. Mixing is rather the process used at the heart of coinjoin. Also, one must not confuse mixing through coinjoins with mixing through a central actor who takes possession of the bitcoins during the process. That has nothing to do with coinjoin, where the user never loses control of their bitcoins during the process.*

entries.title: COINJOIN COORDINATOR
entries.body: Central server that connects users wishing to do coinjoins and coordinates the construction of collaborative transactions, without being able to link the inputs to each user's specific outputs. This is possible through the use of Chaum blind signatures and the Tor network. Unlike a traditional bitcoin mixer, the coinjoin coordinator never takes possession of the participants' bitcoins and is not able to link the inputs and the outputs.

entries.title: COINJUMBLE
entries.body: Software developed by Chris Belcher and launched in August 2014, designed to make coinjoins easier to use with a *GUI*. Unlike other coinjoin implementations of the time, which required participants to want to perform a coinjoin simultaneously, CoinJumble made it possible to share transaction parts asynchronously. Users could exchange through external communication channels to share the encoded transaction parts. Today, CoinJumble is no longer used.

entries.title: COINKITE
entries.body:
Canadian company founded in 2012, specialized in the manufacture of security hardware for Bitcoin. Coinkite is mainly known for the Coldcard, a *hardware wallet* designed specifically for the secure storage of keys. The Coldcard stands out for its minimalist approach focused exclusively on Bitcoin, its air-gapped operation (disconnected from any network), and its many advanced security features.

Coinkite also develops other products such as the Blockclock, a clock that displays the bitcoin price and the block height, as well as the SatsCard and the TapSigner, NFC cards that can store or sign Bitcoin transactions.

entries.title: COINMUX
entries.body: Coinjoin implementation developed in 2014. Coinmux is a decentralized and trustless bitcoin mixing protocol, which requires neither trust between participants nor the intervention of a central actor. The software pools the bitcoins of several users into a single transaction, where each output has identical amounts, which makes it possible to break the links between the inputs and the outputs. The Coinmux protocol ensures that users keep control of their funds throughout the process, by having the transactions signed only when the inputs and outputs correspond exactly to what was agreed. Today, this protocol is no longer used.

entries.title: COINOS
entries.body: Web application (PWA) that allows sending, receiving and accepting bitcoin payments via on-chain, Lightning Network, Liquid and Ecash, directly from a browser. Coinos is aimed at individuals and merchants, with point-of-sale features and a Nostr integration. The platform is custodial.

entries.title: COINS/
entries.body: Name of the old folder used in Bitcoin Core to store the UTXO set, replaced by the `chainstate/` folder in version 0.8.0.

entries.title: COINSHUFFLE
entries.body: Bitcoin mixing protocol proposed in 2014 by Tim Ruffing, Pedro Moreno-Sanchez and Aniket Kate, inspired by the idea formalized by Gregory Maxwell. CoinShuffle makes it possible to cut the history of coins without requiring a trusted third party. The protocol ensures that no participant can link the inputs to the outputs of the other participants. This concept was never widely adopted, as privacy techniques such as the *Chaumian coinjoin* are preferred to it.

entries.title: COINSWAP
entries.body:
Protocol allowing a secret transfer of ownership between users. This method aims to transfer the possession of bitcoins from one person to another, and vice versa, without this exchange being explicitly visible on the blockchain. Coinswap uses smart contracts to carry out the transfer without any need for trust between the parties.

Let's imagine a naive example (which does not work) with Alice and Bob. Alice holds 1 BTC secured with the private key `A`, and Bob also holds 1, secured with the private key `B`. They could theoretically exchange their private keys via an external communication channel to carry out a secret transfer. However, this naive method presents a high risk in terms of trust. Nothing prevents Alice from keeping a copy of the private key `A` after the exchange and using it later to steal the bitcoins, once the key is in Bob's hands. Moreover, there is no guarantee preventing Alice from receiving Bob's private key `B` and never passing on her private key `A` in exchange. This exchange therefore relies on excessive trust between the parties and proves ineffective at ensuring a secret transfer of ownership in a secure manner.

To solve these problems and allow a coinswap between parties who do not trust each other, we will instead use smart contract systems that make the exchange “atomic”. One can use HTLCs (*Hash Time-Locked Contracts*) or PTLCs (*Point Time-Locked Contracts*). These two protocols work in a similar way, using a timelock system that guarantees that the exchange is either successfully completed or entirely canceled, which protects the integrity of both parties' funds. The main difference between HTLCs and PTLCs is that HTLCs use hashes and preimages to secure the transaction, whereas PTLCs use Adaptor Signatures.

In a coinswap scenario using an HTLC or a PTLC between Alice and Bob, the exchange takes place securely: either it succeeds and each receives the other's BTC, or it fails and each keeps their own BTC. It is thus impossible for either party to cheat or to steal the other's BTC. 

The use of Adaptor Signatures is particularly interesting in this context, because it makes it possible to do without traditional scripts (this is a mechanism sometimes referred to as “_scriptless scripts_”). This characteristic makes it possible to reduce the fees associated with the exchange. Another major advantage of Adaptor Signatures is that they do not require the use of a hash common to both parties of the transaction, which thus avoids revealing a direct link between them in certain types of exchanges.

entries.title: COLD WALLET
entries.body:
Synonym of “hardware wallet”. A hardware wallet is an electronic device dedicated to securing and managing the private keys of a Bitcoin wallet. These devices are designed to provide enhanced security compared to software wallets, which reside on general-purpose machines directly connected to the internet. Hardware wallets store the mnemonic phrase offline, on hardware that has a tiny attack surface, which isolates it from potentially vulnerable environments. 

When a transaction is made, the hardware wallet signs the transaction inside the device itself, without exposing the private key to the outside. Once the transaction is signed, it is broadcast to the Bitcoin network to be confirmed and included in the blockchain. Among the most popular hardware wallet models, one can mention: Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard, Passport, BitBox, Satochip, Jade or SeedSigner (non-exhaustive list).

*The hardware wallet can be expressed in different ways in French. Some speak of “portefeuille matériel” (hardware wallet) or “portefeuille froid” (cold wallet). Others prefer that the term “périphérique de signature” be used, or “signing device” in English, in order to avoid giving the impression that the bitcoins are physically located in the wallet.*

entries.title: COLDCARD
entries.body:
Family of *hardware wallets* made by the Canadian company Coinkite, designed exclusively for Bitcoin. Coldcards stand out for their maximum-security approach: they are fully *air-gapped*, meaning they can operate without ever being connected to a computer, exchanging transactions via a microSD card, NFC or the exchange of QR codes. Coldcards integrate *secure elements* to protect private keys against physical access. They offer many advanced security features such as, for example, the “Brick Me PIN” (which destroys the data) and the “Duress PIN” (which opens a decoy wallet).

There are several different Coldcards:
* The MK sub-family (MK3, MK4), which has a numeric keypad only, a small screen, and no camera to scan QR codes;
* The Q sub-family, the brand's top-of-the-range product, with a QR code reader, a battery compartment and a full QWERTY keyboard.

entries.title: COLLATERAL
entries.body:
Asset given as a guarantee by a borrower to a lender to secure a loan or a financial obligation. In the event of the borrower's default, the lender can seize the collateral to cover their loss. This mechanism reduces counterparty risk and makes it possible to access more favorable borrowing conditions.

In the context of Bitcoin, this term can appear in different situations. Most of the time, it is used in the context of Lombard loans. Entities can thus deposit their bitcoins as collateral to obtain loans in *fiat* currency, which allows them to keep their exposure to bitcoin without having to sell it. It can also make it possible to live off one's bitcoins without selling them, and therefore without triggering a taxable event on capital gains. This type of bitcoin-backed Lombard loan is offered by various platforms.

entries.title: COLORED COINS
entries.body: Method proposed in 2012 by Yoni Assia, Vitalik Buterin and Meni Rosenfeld to represent and manage non-native assets on the Bitcoin blockchain. The idea was to attach metadata to specific transactions, in order to color bitcoins to indicate their association with physical assets. The first working implementation, the Open Assets protocol, was developed by Flavien Charlon in 2013. This protocol made it possible to mark bitcoins using `OP_RETURN`.

entries.title: COMMIT
entries.body: In the context of Git, represents a snapshot of the changes made to the set of files in a repository. Each commit is identified by a unique hash and includes a descriptive message, the identity of the author and the date. It makes it possible to track the evolution of the project and to return to earlier states if necessary.

entries.title: COMMITMENT
entries.body:
A Commitment (in the cryptographic sense) is a mathematical object, denoted `C`, derived deterministically from an operation on a structured piece of data `m` (the message) and a random value `r`. We write:
```math
C\ =\ commit(m,\ r)
```
This mechanism comprises two main operations:
* `Commit`: a cryptographic function is applied to a message `m` and to a randomness `r` to produce `C`;
* `Verify`: `C`, the message `m` and the value `r` are used to verify that this commitment is correct. The function returns `Vrai` or `Faux`.

A commitment must satisfy two properties:
* `Binding`: it must be impossible to find a pair `(m', r')` with `m' \neq m` such that:
```math
commit(m',\ r')\ =\ C
```
* `Hiding`: knowledge of `C` must not reveal the content of `m`.

In the case of the RGB protocol, a commitment is included in a Bitcoin transaction in order to prove the existence of certain information at a given moment, without revealing that information itself.

entries.title: COMMITMENT FEE
entries.body:
Fee included in the commitment transaction (*commitment transaction*) of a Lightning channel. This transaction allows each participant to recover their funds in the event of a unilateral closure of the channel. To be confirmed within a reasonable time, it must include sufficient mining fees.

With the introduction of *anchor channels*, the *commitment fee* can be set at a very low amount during channel negotiation. Indeed, *anchor outputs* make it possible to increase the fees at the time the commitment transaction is actually broadcast by attaching an additional UTXO to it via the CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*) mechanism. This avoids overestimating the fees when the channel is created, while guaranteeing quick confirmation in the event of a forced closure.

entries.title: COMPACT BLOCK FILTERS
entries.body:
Mechanism allowing light clients to check whether a block contains transactions concerning them, without downloading the entire blockchain and without revealing their addresses to a third-party node. Unlike the Bloom filters of BIP-0037, where the client sends a filter to a full node (thereby exposing its data), here it is the full nodes that generate deterministic filters for each block. The client downloads them, tests them locally, then retrieves the full blocks only in the event of a match.

The filters are built according to BIP-0158 using *Golomb-Coded Sets* (GCS), a probabilistic structure more compact than Bloom filters. The peer-to-peer distribution protocol is defined in BIP-0157, which introduces dedicated messages (`getcfilters`, `cfilter`, `getcfheaders`...) as well as a system of chained headers making it possible to verify the authenticity of the filters received. A client with at least one honest peer can thus detect any invalid filter.

This mechanism offers better privacy, since blocks can be downloaded from any source, and reduces the computational load imposed on full nodes. In return, the bandwidth consumed in normal operation is higher than that of BIP-0037.

entries.title: COMPACT BLOCK RELAY
entries.body: Protocol introduced in Bitcoin Core in 2016 via BIP-0152, which offers a bandwidth-saving method for network nodes. *Compact Block Relay* makes it possible to communicate block information in a compact way, based on the assumption that nodes already have a large share of the transactions of a recent block in their mempool. Rather than transmitting every transaction in full, which would be redundant, *Compact Block Relay* proposes sending only short identifiers for the transactions already known to peers, accompanied by a few selected transactions (notably the coinbase transaction and those the node is likely not to know). The node can then ask its peers for any missing transactions. *Compact Block Relay* thus reduces the amount of data exchanged during block propagation, which in turn reduces bandwidth spikes and improves the overall efficiency of the network.

entries.title: COMPACTSIZE
COMPRESSED PUBLIC KEY
entries.body:
A public key is used in scripts (either directly as a public key, or in the form of an address) to receive and secure bitcoins. A raw public key is represented by a point on an elliptic curve, made up of two coordinates (`x, y`) each of 256 bits. In raw format, a public key is therefore 512 bits long, not counting the extra byte that identifies the format. A compressed public key, on the other hand, is a more compact way of representing a public key. It uses only the `x` coordinate and a prefix (`02` or `03`) that indicates the parity of the `y` coordinate (even or odd). 

If we simplify this to the field of real numbers, since the elliptic curve is symmetric about the x-axis, for any point `P` (`x, y`) on the curve, there exists a point `P'` (`x, -y`) that will also be on this same curve. This means that for each `x` there are only two possible values of `y`, one positive and one negative. For example, for a given x-coordinate `x`, there would be two points `P_1` and `P_2` on the elliptic curve, which share the same x-coordinate but have opposite y-coordinates:

![Elliptic curve symmetric about the x-axis: for a given x-coordinate, two points P1 and P2 exist.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/cle-publique-compressee/assets/image-1.png)
To choose between the two potential points on the curve, we add to `x` a prefix specifying which `y` to choose. This method reduces the size of a public key from 520 bits to only 264 bits (8 bits of prefix + 256 bits for `x`). This representation is known as the compressed form of the public key.

However, in elliptic curve cryptography, we do not use the real numbers, but a finite field of order `p` (a prime number). In this context, the “sign” of `y` is determined by its parity, that is, whether `y` is even or odd. The prefix `0x02` then indicates an even `y`, while `0x03` indicates an odd `y`.

Let us consider the following example of a raw public key (a point on the elliptic curve) in hexadecimal:
```plaintext
K=04678afdb0fe5548271967f1a67130b7105cd6a828e03909a67962e0ea1f61deb649f6bc3f4cef38c4f35504e51ec112de5c384df7ba0b8d578a4c702b6bf11d5f
```

We can isolate the prefix, `x`, and `y`:
```plaintext
Préfixe=04

x=678afdb0fe5548271967f1a67130b7105cd6a828e03909a67962e0ea1f61deb6

y=49f6bc3f4cef38c4f35504e51ec112de5c384df7ba0b8d578a4c702b6bf11d5f
```

To determine the parity of `y`, we look at the last hexadecimal character of `y`:
```plaintext
Base 16 (hexadécimal) : f
Base 10 (décimal) : 15
y est impair
```

The prefix for the compressed public key will be `03`. The compressed public key in hexadecimal becomes:
```plaintext
K=03678afdb0fe5548271967f1a67130b7105cd6a828e03909a67962e0ea1f61deb6
```

entries.title: CONCATENATION
entries.body: In the context of cryptography and computer systems, refers to the process of joining two operands end to end, thus forming a new string of characters or data. This operation is generally written with a symbol of two vertical bars `\Vert`, or with the symbol `\circ`. For example, the concatenation of `45` with `87` will be equal to `4587`. We will write: `45 \Vert 87 = 4587`. The two operands have been put end to end.

entries.title: CONFIDENTIAL TRANSACTIONS
entries.body:
Cryptographic protocol implemented on the Liquid network that makes it possible to hide the amounts and asset types transferred in a transaction, while still allowing network nodes to verify its validity. *Confidential Transactions* rely on Pedersen commitments (Pedersen *commitments*) to conceal the values, and on range proofs (*rangeproofs*) to guarantee that the committed amounts are positive and do not lead to illegitimate money creation.

This mechanism was proposed by Adam Back in 2013, then formalized and implemented by Gregory Maxwell. CTs have been deployed on Liquid since its launch in 2018. The first versions used Borromean ring signatures (Borromean *ring signatures*) for the range proofs, before adopting more efficient proofs such as Bulletproofs.

entries.title: CONFIRMATION
entries.body: Corresponds to the number of blocks whose security a transaction benefits from. When a transaction is broadcast to the Bitcoin network, it is first pending in the nodes' mempools. It is then included in a valid block by a miner. At this stage, the transaction has just been added to the blockchain, so it has one confirmation. When a new block is found on top of the block containing the transaction in question, it will have a second confirmation, and so on. Each new block mined on top of the block containing the transaction constitutes a new confirmation. By counting the number of confirmations of a transaction, one can estimate the risk that it might ultimately be reversed because of a reorganization. The number of confirmations lets us judge the level of immutability of a transaction on the blockchain.

entries.title: CONNECTOR
entries.body:
Special output created in the round transaction of the Ark protocol to guarantee atomicity between the surrender of the old VTXOs (via the *forfeit transactions*) and the creation of the new ones. Without this mechanism, a user signing a forfeit transaction would hand over control of their VTXO to the ASP with no assurance that the round will succeed and that new VTXOs will be created.

Concretely, the round transaction generates, in addition to the tree containing the output VTXOs, a second covenant tree with one leaf per input VTXO. These leaves are the *connector outputs*. They carry no significant economic value, but serve as a cryptographic link: by including a connector output as an input in a forfeit transaction, the latter becomes valid only if the round transaction is confirmed on-chain. If the round fails, the forfeit transaction is invalid and the user keeps their original VTXO. This mechanism ensures that the two operations (forfeit and creation) are inseparable.

entries.title: CONSENSUS
entries.body:
Mechanism by which all nodes of the Bitcoin network come to agree on the shared state of the blockchain. Consensus allows all users to align on a single history of Bitcoin transactions, notably in order to prevent double spending. Bitcoin's consensus mechanism is sometimes called “Nakamoto Consensus”. It relies on proof of work and specifies that all network nodes accept the chain with the greatest amount of accumulated work.

*By extension, some people use “Consensus” to refer to the tacit rules of the Bitcoin protocol.*

entries.title: CONSENSUS CLEANUP
entries.body:
Soft fork proposal (BIP-0054) grouping together several fixes for old vulnerabilities in Bitcoin's consensus rules. Rather than deploying one soft fork per bug, the “Consensus Cleanup” bundles them to share the fixed cost of a consensus change. The proposal, led by Antoine Poinsot and Matt Corallo, targets four distinct problems.

First, the *time warp* attack: by manipulating timestamps at the boundaries of difficulty adjustment periods, a majority attacker can artificially and unfairly reduce the difficulty to its minimum in a few periods. The fix requires that the first block of a period have a timestamp at most 2 hours before that of the previous block, and that the last block have a timestamp at least equal to that of the first (no negative period in time).

Second, block validation time: specifically crafted blocks can take more than an hour to validate on modest hardware. A limit of 2,500 potentially executed signature operations per transaction reduces the worst case by a factor of 40.

Third, the weakness of the Merkle tree: a 64-byte transaction can be confused with an intermediate node of the tree, making it possible to forge inclusion proofs. These transactions are now invalid.

Fourth, the duplication of coinbase transactions: some blocks prior to BIP-0034 contain a valid height commitment for a future block, which could create duplicates starting from block 1,983,702. Requiring a `nLockTime` equal to the height minus one in coinbases permanently eliminates the need for BIP-0030 validation. This BIP currently has “Draft” status.

entries.title: CONSIGNMENT
entries.body:
In the context of the RGB protocol, groups together the data exchanged between the parties, subject to *Client-side Validation*. There are two main categories of *consignments*:
* `Contract Consignment`: provided by the *issuer* (the contract's issuer), it includes the initialization information such as the *Schema*, the *Genesis*, the *Interface* and the *Implementation* of the *Interface*.
* `Transfer Consignment`: provided by the paying party (*payer*). It contains the entire history of state transitions leading to the *terminal consignment* (that is, the final state received by the beneficiary).

These *consignments* are not recorded publicly in the blockchain; they are exchanged directly between the parties concerned over the communication channel of their choice.

entries.title: CONSOLIDATION
entries.body:
Specific transaction in which several small UTXOs are merged as inputs to form a single, larger UTXO as output. This operation is a transaction made to one's own wallet. The goal of consolidation is to take advantage of periods when fees on the Bitcoin network are low to merge several small UTXOs into a single one that is larger in value. In this way, one anticipates mandatory spending in case fees rise, which saves on future transaction fees. 

Indeed, transactions with many inputs are heavier and, consequently, more expensive. Besides the savings that can be made on transaction fees, consolidation is also a form of long-term planning. If your wallet contains very small UTXOs, these can become unusable if the Bitcoin network enters a prolonged period of high fees. For example, if you need to spend a 10,000 sats UTXO but the minimum mining fees amount to 15,000 sats, spending it would exceed the value of the UTXO itself. These small UTXOs then become economically irrational to use and remain unusable as long as fees do not fall. These UTXOs are commonly called “*dust*”. By regularly consolidating your small UTXOs, you reduce this risk associated with fee increases.

However, it is important to note that consolidation transactions are recognizable in chain analysis. Such a transaction indicates a CIOH (*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*), meaning that the inputs of the consolidation transaction are owned by a single entity. This may have privacy implications for the user.

![Consolidation transaction: five small UTXOs merged as inputs to form a single UTXO of 550,000 sats as output.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/consolidation/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: CONTAINER
entries.body: In the context of mining, a container is a modular structure used to house and operate a large number of ASICs. These containers are designed to optimize space, heat management and power supply. They can be equipped with different cooling systems, such as *air cooling*, *hydro cooling* or *immersion cooling*. Their main advantage lies in their mobility and their ability to be deployed quickly, often close to cheap energy sources.

entries.title: CONTRACT OPERATION
CONTRACT PARTICIPANT
CONTRACT RIGHTS
CONTRACT STATE
CONTRIBUTOR
entries.body: A contributor in the context of Bitcoin Core (the majority node implementation on the Bitcoin network) is a person who actively participates in the development of the software by writing code, and by reviewing and testing changes proposed by others. Unlike maintainers, contributors do not have the power to merge changes into the main code; their role is rather to submit *pull requests* (PRs) and to take part in the discussion and validation of these proposals. Any interested individual can become a contributor without needing a nomination or formal approval, which differs from maintainers, who are entrusted with higher administrative and decision-making responsibilities in the project.

entries.title: CONTROL BLOCK
CONTROL BOARD
entries.body: Component in a mining machine that manages and coordinates the device's operations. The control board handles communication between the software and the ASIC chips. It also makes it possible to monitor the hardware's performance and control its temperature.

entries.title: COOKIE
entries.body: File used for RPC (*Remote Procedure Call*) authentication in Bitcoin Core. When bitcoind starts, it generates a unique authentication cookie and stores it in this file. Clients or scripts that want to interact with bitcoind via the RPC interface can use this cookie to authenticate securely. This mechanism allows safe communication between bitcoind and external applications (such as wallet software, for example), without requiring manual management of usernames and passwords. The `.cookie` file is regenerated each time bitcoind restarts and deleted when it shuts down.

entries.title: COOPERATIVE CLOSE
entries.body:
Closing of a Lightning channel carried out with the mutual agreement of both parties. It is the most advantageous closing method: both channel partners jointly sign a closing transaction that redistributes the funds to their respective addresses, without a timelock.

Unlike a forced closure (*force close*), where a unilateral commitment transaction is broadcast and imposes a *timelock* before the funds become accessible, a cooperative close produces a simple transaction. Mining fees are therefore reduced (since they can be adjusted to the current fee market), and the funds are available as soon as the transaction is confirmed.

entries.title: COUNTERPARTY
entries.body: Open source meta-protocol launched in January 2014 that made it possible to create and exchange digital assets directly on the Bitcoin blockchain. Counterparty encodes token metadata in Bitcoin transactions, mainly via multisig outputs or `OP_RETURN`, without modifying the base protocol.

entries.title: COVENANT
entries.body:
Mechanism that makes it possible to impose specific conditions on how a given coin can be spent, including in future transactions. Beyond the conditions usually allowed by the script language on a UTXO, the covenant enforces additional constraints on how to spend that bitcoin coin in subsequent transactions. Technically, a covenant is established when the `scriptPubKey` of a UTXO defines restrictions on the `scriptPubKey` of the outputs of a transaction that spends said UTXO. By broadening the scope of script, covenants would enable many developments on Bitcoin such as the two-way peg of drivechains, the implementation of vaults, or the improvement of overlay systems like Lightning. Covenant proposals are differentiated according to three criteria:
* Their scope;
* Their implementation;
* Their recursiveness.

There are a great many proposals that would allow the use of covenants on Bitcoin. The most advanced in the implementation process are: `OP_CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY` (CTV), `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` (APO) and `OP_VAULT`. Among the other proposals are: `OP_TX`, `OP_TAPLEAFUPDATEVERIFY` (TLUV), `OP_EVICT`, `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK` (CSFS), `OP_CAT`, etc.

To properly understand the concept of covenant, I suggest an analogy: imagine a safe containing €500 in small bills.
