If you manage to unlock this safe with the right key, then you are free to use this money as you see fit. That is Bitcoin's normal situation. Now, imagine that this same safe does not contain €500 in banknotes, but rather meal vouchers of equivalent value. If you succeed in opening this safe, you can make use of that sum. However, your freedom to spend is restricted, because you can only use these vouchers to pay in certain restaurants. Thus, there is a first condition for spending this money, which is to manage to open the safe with the appropriate key. But there is also an additional condition regarding the future use of this sum: it must be spent exclusively in partner restaurants, and not with complete freedom. This system of constraints on future transactions is what we call a covenant.

*In French, there is no term that precisely captures the meaning of the word "covenant". One could speak of a "clause", a "pact", or a "commitment", but this would not correspond exactly to the term "covenant". The latter is in fact borrowed from a legal terminology used to describe a contractual clause imposing persistent obligations on a property.*

entries.title: COVERT ASICBOOST
entries.body: Secret version of AsicBoost. AsicBoost is an algorithmic optimization method for Bitcoin mining. In its Covert version, miners manipulate the Merkle tree rather than the Nonce, which thus reduces the calculations needed for each SHA256 hash by keeping certain data unchanged between hashing attempts. Unlike the Overt version of AsicBoost, the Covert version conceals the use of AsicBoost during the mining process. However, since the introduction of SegWit and its second Merkle tree, this method is no longer effective, because the number of calculations required to use it has become too large compared to a classic mining process.

entries.title: CPFP - CHILD PAY FOR PARENT
entries.body:
Transactional mechanism aimed at speeding up the confirmation of a Bitcoin transaction, just as *Replace-by-Fee* (RBF) does, but on the recipient's side. When a transaction with fees that are too low relative to the market remains stuck in the nodes' mempools and does not confirm quickly enough, the recipient can make a new transaction, spending the bitcoins received in the stuck transaction, even though it is not yet confirmed. This second transaction necessarily requires the first one to be mined in order to be confirmed. Miners are therefore obliged to include both transactions together. The second one will allocate much more in transaction fees than the first, so that the average fee incentivizes miners to include both transactions. The child transaction (the second one) pays for the stuck parent transaction (the first one). This is why it is called a "CPFP".

Thus, CPFP allows the recipient to obtain their funds more quickly despite the low initial fees committed by the sender, unlike RBF (*Replace-by-Fee*), which allows the sender to take the initiative to speed up their own transaction by increasing the fees.

entries.title: CPPSRB
entries.body: Acronym for "*Capped Pay Per Share with Recent Backpay*". It is a method of calculating miner remuneration in the context of mining pools. In this system, the pool pays as many shares as it can each time a block is found, giving priority to the most recent shares. This method makes it possible to guarantee the financial stability of the mining pool, while offering per-task remuneration and encouraging miners to stay connected to the pool to avoid *pool hopping*.

entries.title: CPU - CENTRAL PROCESSING UNIT
entries.body: Main component of a computer responsible for executing the machine instructions of software. In the context of Bitcoin, the CPU was initially used for mining by nodes before being surpassed by mining with GPUs (graphics cards), and then by the use of specialized chips called "ASICs".

entries.title: CRYPTANALYSIS
entries.body: Study of mathematical techniques to attempt to break cryptographic techniques. This includes the processes of searching for errors or weaknesses in the implementation of a cryptographic method or in the cryptographic method itself.

entries.title: CRYPTER
entries.body: This term does not exist. One says "chiffrer".

entries.title: CRYPTO-ASSET
entries.body: Term used in a legal and regulatory context to designate the various types of cryptocurrencies, including bitcoin.

entries.title: CRYPTOCURRENCY
entries.body: Generic qualifier given to any form of money, asset, credit, or digital unit within a computer system in which cryptography is used for exchanges and transactions between users.

entries.title: CRYPTOGRAPHY
entries.body: Discipline embodying the principles, means, and methods for transforming information, notably with mathematical techniques, in order to hide its semantic content, prevent its unauthorized use, ensure its authenticity, or prevent its undetected modification. Cryptography encompasses the use of hash functions, digital signatures, and encryption algorithms.

entries.title: CRYPTOLOGY
entries.body: Mathematical science that deals with cryptanalysis and cryptography.

entries.title: CTUSD - CITREA USD
entries.body: Native stablecoin of the Citrea platform, pegged to the US dollar at a 1:1 parity. ctUSD (*Citrea USD*) is backed by short-term US Treasury bills and cash reserves. It is issued in partnership with MoonPay and relies on the infrastructure of M0, an institutional stablecoin protocol.

entries.title: CURTAILMENT
entries.body: Refers to the voluntary reduction of a mining farm's electricity consumption by shutting down machines. This reduction is part of certain contracts made with electricity producers. When there is an overproduction of energy relative to market demand, miners use this surplus. When there are demand peaks relative to production, miners can reduce their consumption in order to stabilize the grid.

entries.title: CUSTODY
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, refers to the holding and management of the private keys that allow control of bitcoins. BTC *custody* can be provided in two ways: either personally by the user, who keeps the private keys needed to access their bitcoins themselves (what is called "*self-custody*"), or by a third party, such as an exchange platform, where the company holds the private keys and manages the bitcoins on the user's behalf. This second option is riskier than *self-custody*, as it exposes the user's funds to the risks of hacking, bankruptcy, or fraudulent behavior on the part of the custodian.

*In French, the English term "custody" is generally used. It could also be translated as "garde".*

entries.title: CYPHERPUNKS
entries.body:
Informal, international community of people promoting the use of cryptography as a means of ensuring individual freedoms on the Internet. Cypherpunks defend the fundamental right of the individual to protect their privacy, particularly in a context of increasing state surveillance and data exploitation by private entities. Their name comes from the English words *cypher*, "cipher" (in the sense of secret code), and *punk*. It is a calque of the term *cyberpunk*, which designates a literary genre describing a dystopian future where cutting-edge technology is married to the vice and crime of a decaying society.

The cypherpunk movement dates back to the early 1990s, when groups of cryptographers, programmers, and libertarians began discussing the political implications of cryptography during their first meetings in Silicon Valley. The main figure in the community was Tim May, who had written the *Crypto Anarchist Manifesto* in 1988, a founding text of the movement. Among the key moments in cypherpunk history is the founding, in 1992, of the "Cypherpunks mailing list", an email distribution list that served for these discussions. The publication by Eric Hughes in 1993 of *A Cypherpunk's Manifesto*, a document setting out the goals and actions of cypherpunks, was also an important moment.

The idea of an electronic currency that is not based on a central entity, like Bitcoin, is rooted in the philosophy of the cypherpunks. The creation of Bitcoin is often considered a major achievement of this vision, alongside PGP, Tor, and WikiLeaks.

entries.title: DERIVATION PATH
DIFFICULTY TARGET
entries.body:
The difficulty factor, also known as the difficulty target, is a parameter used in the proof of work (*Proof of Work*, PoW) consensus mechanism on Bitcoin. The target represents a numerical value that determines how difficult it is for miners to solve a specific cryptographic problem, called proof of work, when creating a new block on the blockchain. 

The difficulty target is an adjustable 256-bit (32-byte) number that sets an acceptability limit for the hash of the block header. In other words, for a block to be valid, the hash of its header with `SHA256d` (double `SHA256`) must be numerically less than or equal to the difficulty target. Proof of work consists of modifying the `nonce` field of the block header or of the coinbase transaction until the resulting hash is lower than the target value. 

This target is adjusted every 2016 blocks (approximately every two weeks), during an event called an "adjustment". The difficulty factor is recalculated based on the time it took to mine the previous 2016 blocks. If the total time is less than two weeks, the difficulty increases by adjusting the target downward. If the total time is greater than two weeks, the difficulty decreases by adjusting the target upward. The goal is to keep the average mining time per block at 10 minutes. This time between each block helps avoid splits in the Bitcoin network, which result in a waste of computing power. The difficulty target is found in each block header, within the `nBits` field. Since this field is reduced to 32 bits and the target is actually 256 bits, the target is compacted into a less precise scientific format.

![Candidate block hashed with SHA256d: the hash is valid if it falls below the target adjusted every 2016 blocks.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/cible-de-difficulte/assets/image-1.png)

*The difficulty target is sometimes also called the "difficulty factor". By extension, it can be referred to through its encoding in block headers with the term "nBits".*

entries.title: DIGEST / HASH
entries.body: In cryptography, refers to the result (or *output*) produced by applying a cryptographic hash function to a set of data. The digest is a fixed-size string of characters, generally represented as a series of digits and letters in hexadecimal (base 16) notation. This result has the particularity of being almost unique and specific to the input data, so that a minimal change in the input will produce a completely different digest. Cryptographic hash functions are designed to be one-way and collision-resistant, making it very difficult to recover the original data from the digest or to find two distinct inputs producing the same digest.

entries.title: ELLIPTIC CURVE
entries.body: In the context of cryptography, an elliptic curve is an algebraic curve defined by an equation of the form `y^2 = x^3 + ax + b`. These curves are used in elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), which is a public-key cryptography method for creating encryption algorithms, digital signatures, and key exchange. In the context of Bitcoin, the ECDSA (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*) or the Schnorr protocol are used with the `secp256k1` curve. This curve was chosen for its performance and security properties. These algorithms are used to generate public keys from private keys, as well as to sign transactions, and therefore unlock bitcoins.

entries.title: ENCRYPT - ENCRYPTION
entries.body: A cryptographic method for converting raw information into encrypted information. Encrypted information hides the original meaning of the data to prevent it from being known. Encryption consists of a series of transformations performed on the original information using a key. If these transformations are reversible, the corresponding inverse process is called "decryption", and it makes it possible to restore the information to its raw state.

entries.title: EXTENDED KEY
EXTERNAL KEYCHAIN
entries.body:
In the derivation of hierarchical deterministic wallets, the external keychain is a derivation branch used to generate receiving addresses intended to receive payments coming from the outside, that is, from another wallet. Each account as defined at depth 3 has two keychains at depth 4: an external keychain and an internal keychain (also called “change”). The external keychain is derived with an index of `/0/`.  The external keychain derives addresses intended to be shared publicly, that is, the addresses we are offered when we click the “receive” button in our wallet software.

![BIP-84 tree with an arrow pointing to the Chains level, where each account splits into an external chain /0 and an internal chain /1.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/chaine-externe/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: INTERNAL KEYCHAIN
entries.body:
In the derivation of hierarchical deterministic wallets, the internal keychain is a derivation branch used to generate receiving addresses intended to receive payments coming from the same wallet, that is, only change addresses. Each account as defined at depth 3 has two keychains at depth 4: an external keychain and an internal keychain (also called “change”). The internal keychain is derived with an index of `/1/`.

![BIP-84 tree with an arrow pointing to the Chains level, where the internal chain /1 derives only change addresses.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/chaine-interne/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: LEGAL TENDER
entries.body:
Legal status assigned to a currency by a state, which obliges any creditor to accept it as payment of a debt. A currency that is legal tender cannot be refused for the settlement of an obligation denominated in the national currency.

In September 2021, El Salvador became the first country to grant legal tender status to bitcoin alongside the US dollar. This decision provoked mixed reactions: some bitcoiners see it as a precedent for Bitcoin adoption, while others criticized the obligation imposed on merchants to accept it, which has since been abandoned.

entries.title: LIGHTNING CHANNEL CAPACITY
entries.body: The quantity of bitcoins locked in a multisig address that represents a payment channel on the Lightning Network. A channel's capacity is therefore the maximum quantity of sats that can be transmitted through that specific channel. It is defined at the time the channel is created by the sum of the funds the parties commit to the channel. The “*inbound capacity*”, or “incoming capacity”, refers to the maximum quantity of bitcoins a node can receive through a channel. The “*outbound capacity*”, or “outgoing capacity”, represents the maximum quantity of bitcoins a node can send through a specific channel.

entries.title: MASTER CHAIN CODE
entries.body: Designates the chain code associated with the wallet's master key, at the base of the derivation tree of all keys.

entries.title: MASTER KEY
entries.body:
In the context of HD (hierarchical deterministic) wallets, the master private key is a unique private key derived from the wallet's seed. To obtain the master key, the `HMAC-SHA512` function is applied to the seed, literally using the words "*Bitcoin seed*" as the key. The result of this operation gives a 512-bit output, of which the first 256 bits constitute the master key, and the remaining 256 bits form the master chain code. The master key and the master chain code serve as the starting point for deriving all the child private and public keys in the tree structure of the HD wallet. The master private key is therefore at derivation depth 0.

![BIP-84 tree with an arrow pointing to the master key m, the single starting point of the entire HD derivation.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/cle-maitresse/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: MERCHANT
entries.body: Any natural or legal person who agrees to exchange a good or a service for bitcoins. It is these merchants who give the bitcoin currency its usefulness. The more widely a currency is accepted by a broad range of merchants, the more useful it becomes for individuals. Since merchants have the ability to determine the usefulness of a currency by agreeing to exchange it for goods and services, in the case of Bitcoin they also have considerable weight in the choice of consensus rules. Each has a certain power proportional to the economic activity they are able to bring to a fork. Among merchants, there are obviously businesses, but also exchange platforms, miners and users.

entries.title: PAYLOAD
PAYMENT CHANNEL
entries.body: In the context of the Lightning Network, a payment channel is a bidirectional connection between two Lightning nodes that allows bitcoins to be exchanged off-chain. On-chain, a payment channel is represented by a 2/2 multisig address held by the two participants. The payment channel requires one on-chain transaction to open it and another to close it. Between these two events, the channel's users can carry out a very large number of off-chain bitcoin exchanges, on the Lightning Network, without requiring on-chain activity. On Lightning, it is possible to route a payment through several channels and several nodes, in order to send bitcoins without necessarily opening a direct channel with the recipient.

entries.title: PRIMARY PATH
entries.body: In a wallet software using Miniscript, such as Liana for example, the primary path refers to the set of keys allowing immediate spending of funds, without any time condition. This path is always accessible and is used for the day-to-day management of bitcoins, without requiring any waiting (*timelock*), unlike recovery paths. Let's take the example of a script that includes 2 distinct keys: key A, which authorizes the immediate spending of the bitcoins, and key B, which allows them to be spent after a delay defined by a *timelock* of 52,560 blocks. In this example, key A comes from the primary path, while key B comes from the recovery path.

entries.title: PRIVATE KEY
entries.body:
A private key is a fundamental element of asymmetric cryptography. It is a number (256 bits in the case of Bitcoin) that represents a cryptographic secret. This key is used to digitally sign transactions and to prove possession of a Bitcoin public key (and by extension, of a receiving address) by satisfying a `scriptPubKey`. Private keys therefore make it possible to spend bitcoins by unlocking the UTXOs associated with the corresponding public key. Private keys must be kept strictly confidential, because their disclosure could allow malicious third parties to take control of the associated funds. 

In the Bitcoin system, the private key is linked to a public key through an elliptic curve digital signature algorithm (ECDSA or Schnorr). The public key is derived from the private key, but the reverse is practically impossible to achieve because of the computational difficulty inherent in solving the underlying mathematical problem (the discrete logarithm problem). The public key is generally used to generate a Bitcoin address, which serves to lock bitcoins using a script. In cryptography, private keys are often random or pseudo-random numbers. In the specific context of Bitcoin hierarchical deterministic wallets, private keys are derived deterministically from the seed. Private keys are frequently confused with the seed or with the recovery phrase (mnemonic). However, these elements are quite different.

*In French, a private key is called "clé privée". This term is sometimes abbreviated as "privkey", or "PV".*

entries.title: PUBLIC KEY
entries.body:
The public key is an element used in asymmetric cryptography. It is generated from a private key using an irreversible mathematical function. On Bitcoin, public keys are derived from their associated private key using the ECDSA or Schnorr elliptic curve digital signature algorithms. The public key, unlike the private key, can be shared freely without compromising the security of funds. Within the Bitcoin protocol, the public key serves as the basis for creating a Bitcoin address, which is then used to create spending conditions on a UTXO using a `scriptPubKey`. Public keys are frequently confused with the master key or with extended keys (`xpub`...). Yet these elements are quite different.

*In French, a public key is called “clé publique”. This term is sometimes abbreviated as “pubkey”, or “PK”.*

entries.title: RECOVERY PATH
entries.body: In a wallet software using Miniscript, such as Liana for example, the recovery path(s) refer to sets of keys that only become operational after a period of inactivity defined in the script that locks the bitcoins (*timelock*). Recovery paths can only be used once the *timelocks* have passed, and thus offer a method of recovering funds when the primary path is not available. Let's take the example of a script that includes 2 distinct keys: key A, which authorizes the immediate spending of the bitcoins, and key B, which allows them to be spent after a delay defined by a *timelock* of 52,560 blocks. In this example, key A comes from the primary path, while key B comes from the recovery path.

entries.title: REUSABLE PAYMENT CODE
REVOCATION KEY
entries.body:
A cryptographic key used in the Lightning Network to allow the punishment of a peer who publishes an old channel state. Each commitment transaction contains a `to_local` output that offers two spending paths:
* one subject to a relative delay (`OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY`) for the owner,
* the other immediately spendable by the counterparty if it holds the corresponding revocation key.

The revocation key is built collaboratively. For a given commitment transaction, Alice provides a commitment point (`C_A`) and Bob provides a revocation base point (`R_B`). The revocation public key is calculated as follows:
```math
Rev\ =\ R_B \cdot SHA256(R_B\ \Vert\ C_A)\ +\ C_A \cdot SHA256(C_A\ \Vert\ R_B)
```
Neither Alice nor Bob can derive the corresponding private key alone. When the channel state is updated, Alice reveals the secret `c_A` associated with her commitment point. Bob can then combine `c_A` with his own secret `r_B` to obtain the revocation private key and, if necessary, build a penalty transaction.

entries.title: RGB CONTRACT
entries.body: Refers to a set of rights executed digitally between several actors via the RGB protocol. It has an active state and a business logic, defined by a *Schema*, which specifies which operations are authorized (transfers, extensions, etc.). The state of a contract, as well as the validity rules, are expressed in the *Schema*. At any time, the contract evolves only in accordance with what is permitted by this *Schema* and by the validation scripts (executed, for example, in AluVM).

entries.title: SMART CONTRACT
entries.body:
Program that executes automatically when certain predefined conditions are met. A smart contract is thus a set of clauses between several parties that can be fulfilled without requiring the intervention of a trusted third party. These contracts generally trigger specific actions such as a transfer of bitcoins.

*In French, the term “contrat autonome” is also sometimes used.*
